title: Giant Rhino Herds Roamed North America: New Fossil Evidence
text:
Uncover the secrets of the past! New research delves into the migration patterns of ancient rhinos, offering engaging insights into the lives of Teleoceras major at the Ashfall Fossil Beds . Discover how scientists are using isotope analysis to solve the mystery of why so many rhinos perished in one location, and what these findings reveal about their ancient world.
Ancient Rhino Migration Patterns Uncovered at Ashfall Fossil Beds Nebraska, April 9, 2025
A Graveyard of Giants: Unearthing teh Secrets of teleoceras major Paleontologists are piecing together the lives of extinct rhinos at the Ashfall Fossil Beds in Nebraska, a site preserving the remains of more than 100 Teleoceras major individuals. These rhinos, wich roamed North America from 17.5 to 5 million years ago, met their end at a watering hole, entombed by ash from a Yellowstone supervolcano eruption.
Herd of Teleoceras rhinos. Image credit: Jay Matternes / Smithsonian Museum. the Central Question: Why So Manny Rhinos in One Place? Since the 1971 finding of the rhinos at Ashfall Fossil Beds State Historical Park, a key question has persisted: What drew so many of these animals to a single location? Did they migrate from afar, seeking refuge from the volcanic eruption and it’s suffocating ash?
Isotopic Clues: Unlocking Movement Patterns Researchers at the University of Minnesota have turned to isotope analysis to understand the movements of these long-extinct creatures. By examining ratios of strontium, oxygen, and carbon isotopes in Teleoceras major teeth, they are reconstructing the animals’ journeys across ancient landscapes.
Strontium: Reveals foraging locations based on soil and bedrock composition. Carbon: Helps reconstruct the ancient surroundings, indicating vegetation types and moisture levels. According to Clark Ward, a researcher at the University of Minnesota, the findings challenge previous assumptions. We found they didn’t move very much. He added, We didn’t find evidence for seasonal migration or any evidence of a response to the disaster.
Teleoceras major : A Hippo-Like Rhino Teleoceras major was a unique rhino species, characterized by:
A single horn. A barrel-shaped body. Stubby, hippo-like legs. Like hippos, these rhinos primarily grazed on grass and likely spent considerable time in and around water. Their large size offered protection from most predators during the Miocene epoch . However,calves were vulnerable to bone-crushing dogs,hyena-like predators whose tracks and scavenging marks have been found at the Ashfall site.
The Yellowstone Connection: A Volcanic Catastrophe Yellowstone’s volcanic activity has shaped the landscape for millions of years. During one eruption, ash traveled more than 700 miles, blanketing Nebraska in a thick layer. Ward explained the impact: Ash from the eruption easily would have traveled 1,127 km (700 miles) across what is now Nebraska where it piled up like snow nearly a foot deep in places. He further noted, But windblown ash continued to fall on Nebraska long after the initial eruption.That ash would have covered everything: the grass,leaves and water.
Implications for Paleoecology The research underscores the importance of understanding how extinct animals interacted with their environments. Reconstructing how extinct ungulates utilized ancient landscapes provides critically important context for understanding their paleoecology and sociality and also the environments they inhabited, the scientists concluded.
The findings were published in Scientific Reports .
